Cease
sēs
v. (to stop; to leave off; to come to an end; rendering Hebrew chadal, shabath, Greek pauo)
From Latin cesso, to loiter or leave off. Scripture measures men by what they will not cease from — prayer, chiefly — and comforts them with what will one day cease: war, trouble, and the weariness of the labouring saint.

Biblical Definition

To cease is to stop, and Scripture uses the word to mark both a duty and a hope. Samuel makes ceasing from intercession a sin against God, which is a remarkable way to state the obligation: “God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you: but I will teach you the good and the right way” (1 Samuel 12:23). He is speaking to a people who had just rejected his counsel; the prayer continues anyway, and abandoning it would have been the transgression. Paul compresses the same duty into two words: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). The other use is promissory, and it names what God will bring to an end. Of war: “He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire” (Psalm 46:9). Of the trouble that follows the righteous through this life, Job speaks from the depth of his affliction and looks past it to the grave: “There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest” (Job 3:17). The pattern is consistent: what God commands is unceasing, and what wearies His people is not.

Webster 1828 Definition

To stop; to leave off; to desist; to come to an end. Scripture forbids ceasing from prayer, calling it sin, and promises the ceasing of war, of trouble, and of the weariness that presses upon the saints.

expand to see more

CEASE, v.i. [L. cesso, to loiter, to cease.] To stop moving, acting or speaking; to leave off; to give over; as, cease from anger.

2. To fail; to be wanting; to be at an end; as, the poor shall never cease out of the land.

3. To be forgotten; to become extinct; to pass away.

CEASE, v.t. To put a stop to; to put an end to; as, cease this strife.

CEASELESS, a. Without a stop or pause; incessant; continual; without intermission.

CEASING, ppr. Leaving off; desisting; putting an end to.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 12:23 — "Moreover as for me, God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you: but I will teach you the good and the right way:"

1 Thessalonians 5:17 — "Pray without ceasing."

Psalm 46:9 — "He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire."

Job 3:17 — "There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest."

Modern Corruption

Persevering prayer has been demoted to a discipline men adopt when it suits them, though Samuel calls ceasing from it a sin against the LORD — and that for a people who had just refused his counsel.

expand to see more

1 Samuel 12:23 is a harder verse than its familiarity suggests. Samuel has been rejected as judge, the people have demanded a king against the counsel of God, and the prophet's response is that ceasing to pray for them would be sin. Modern practice quietly assumes the reverse: that intercession is owed to those who receive it well, and that a people who will not hear may be left to themselves. The Apostle's without ceasing forecloses the calculation entirely. Prayer that stops when it is unappreciated, unanswered, or unreciprocated has been governed by something other than the command.

The second drift is subtler and touches the promises. Psalm 46:9 and Job 3:17 speak of a ceasing that God will accomplish, not one that men engineer, and the age is impatient with that distinction. Where the cessation of war and trouble is treated as a project to be completed by human effort within history, disappointment is guaranteed and the promise is discredited by the failure of a scheme Scripture never proposed. The believer's posture is the one both texts model: labour and pray now without ceasing, and expect the ceasing of war and weariness from the hand that breaks the bow.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chadal (to cease, forbear, leave off) and shabath (to rest, desist) supply the Old Testament sense; Greek pauo (to stop) and the adverb adialeiptos (without ceasing) frame the New Testament command.

expand to see more

Hebrew chadal (H2308) — to cease, to forbear, to leave off; the verb of Samuel's refusal to stop praying.

Hebrew shabath (H7673) — to cease, to rest, to desist; the root behind the sabbath and behind wars made to cease.

Greek pauo (G3973) — to make to cease, to stop; used of tongues which shall cease in 1 Corinthians 13:8.

Greek adialeiptos (G89) — unceasing, without intermission; the single adverb of 1 Thessalonians 5:17.

Greek ekkakeo (G1573) — to lose heart, to faint; the failing our Lord opposes to praying always.

Usage

"“God forbid that I should sin… in ceasing to pray for you” — abandoning intercession is named as sin."

"“Pray without ceasing” — the command admits no season of exemption."

"“There the weary be at rest” — the ceasing of trouble is God's work, not man's project."
